\chapter{Who Someone Is --- Neighbour, Friend, Teacher, Nurse, Cook}
\label{ch:quien-es}
\hlchaptermodality{285}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say who someone is in Spanish — the neighbour, a friend, the teacher, the nurse, the cook.}

Complete ES-C285-cocinero: name all five people, and say what each name is really describing.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[el vecino]{el vecino — the man from your own street}

\label{lesson:ES-C285-vecino}



\begin{quote}
Before a new run: what does \emph{por supuesto} say has happened to the thing? (It was placed underneath — assumed.) And what is inside \emph{acuerdo}? (The heart.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la casa — the house this person lives near.
  \item hola — what you say to him over the fence.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ve-CI-no}, stress in the middle. The \emph{c} before \emph{i} is the \emph{th} of \emph{think} in much of Spain and an \emph{s} elsewhere. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el vecino} — \textquotedblleft{}the neighbour.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{vicinus}, from \textbf{vicus}: a village, a row of houses, a block of a town. A \emph{vicinus} is a person off your own street, and the word names the street rather than the person.

English has the abstract end of it. \textbf{Vicinity} is nearness — the quality of sharing a \emph{vicus}. And \emph{vicus} itself was borrowed into Old English early as \emph{wic}, a settlement, which is the \emph{-wich} still sitting on the end of Norwich and Ipswich.

English \textbf{neighbour} describes the same man quite differently: \emph{neah}, near, plus \emph{gebur}, a dweller. A near-dweller. Two languages, one person, and two pictures — a street against a distance.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Every name for a person is a description that stopped being one.

Hold on to that for the next four. None of them will name the human being directly; each names a place, a feeling, a comparison or an act, and lets the ending turn it into somebody.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el vecino}, then \emph{la vecina}
  \item \emph{mi vecino}
  \item \emph{el vecino} and \emph{la casa}, and hear the street inside the first
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{vicus}? (A village or a row of houses.) What does English \emph{neighbour} describe instead? (A near-dweller — distance, not a street.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la amiga]{la amiga — the same root as amable, a short way back}

\label{lesson:ES-C285-amiga}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what does \emph{vecino} actually name? (The street, not the man.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item amable — the same Latin root, met a short while ago.
  \item el vecino — the person before this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la a-MI-ga}, stress on the \emph{mi}. The two \emph{a} sounds at the join run together in ordinary speech. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la amiga} — \textquotedblleft{}a friend,\textquotedblright{} of a woman.

Latin \textbf{amica}, and underneath it is \textbf{amare}, to love — the very \emph{amare} that gave you \emph{amable} not long ago. Latin made the kind person and the friend out of one root, and Spanish inherited both without noticing the family resemblance.

English \textbf{amicable} is \emph{amicabilis}, friend-like, and an \textbf{amicus curiae} in a courtroom is a friend of the court. But English \textbf{friend} is Germanic, from a word for loving that has otherwise disappeared — so both languages built the friend out of a love word, and then lost the source in one case and kept it in the other.

Note the article: \emph{la amiga}, and not the \emph{el} that \emph{agua} takes. That swap needs the stress on the first \emph{a}, and here it falls on the \emph{i}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A root you have already spent is cheaper than a new one.

\emph{Amable} and \emph{amiga} cost you one Latin root between them. When two words share a root, learning the second is mostly remembering the first.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la amiga}, then \emph{el amigo}
  \item \emph{amable} and \emph{amiga}, and hear \emph{amare} in both
  \item \emph{mi amiga}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which root is under \emph{amiga}? (\emph{Amare}, to love.) Which other word of yours is built on it? (\emph{Amable}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el maestro]{el maestro — the one who is more}

\label{lesson:ES-C285-maestro}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: which root is under \emph{amiga}? (\emph{Amare}, to love.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el estudiante — the person this one stands in front of.
  \item la amiga — the person before this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{ma-ES-tro}, stress on the \emph{es}. The \emph{a} and the \emph{e} stay separate — three syllables, not two. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el maestro} — \textquotedblleft{}the teacher.\textquotedblright{}

Latin \textbf{magister}, built on \textbf{magis}, more. Beside it Latin kept \textbf{minister}, built on \textbf{minus}, less. The two were made as a matched pair: the one who is more and the one who is less, a master and a servant.

Both reached English and drifted so far apart that the pairing is invisible. On one side a \textbf{master}, a \textbf{mister} (the same word worn down), a \textbf{magistrate} and a \textbf{magnate}. On the other a \textbf{minister} and to \textbf{administer} — which is to serve towards something.

Spanish kept \emph{maestro} for the schoolteacher and has \emph{profesor} as well, which you already have. The two are not rivals: one teaches children and the other teaches a subject.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
A comparison can harden into a job.

\emph{Magis} and \emph{minus} are not people; they are more and less. Latin turned both into titles, and two thousand years later one of them signs your school report and the other runs a government.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el maestro}, then \emph{la maestra}
  \item \emph{maestro} and \emph{master}, and hear the \emph{magis} in both
  \item \emph{el maestro} and \emph{el estudiante} together
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is \emph{magis}? (More.) What was \emph{minister} built on? (\emph{Minus}, less.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la enfermera]{la enfermera — named after the patient}

\label{lesson:ES-C285-enfermera}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: what is \emph{magis}? (More.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item el maestro — the person before this one.
  \item la cabeza — a body word, useful when you say what is wrong.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{en-fer-ME-ra}, stress on the \emph{me}. Both \emph{r} sounds are single taps, neither rolled. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{la enfermera} — \textquotedblleft{}the nurse.\textquotedblright{}

From \textbf{enfermo}, ill, and that is Latin \textbf{infirmus}: \emph{in-}, not, plus \textbf{firmus}, firm. The ill person is the one who is no longer steady on his feet. And the nurse is named after the patient rather than after the work.

English kept \emph{infirmus} twice over — \textbf{infirm} for the person, an \textbf{infirmary} for the room they are put in. \textbf{Firm} itself is the same \emph{firmus}, and to \textbf{confirm} is to make a thing firm along with somebody else.

English \textbf{nurse} went the other way entirely. It is \emph{nutrire}, to feed: the wet-nurse came first and the hospital a long time afterwards. One language named the helper after the illness, the other after the milk.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Four people, and four different things being described.

A street, a word for loving, a comparison, and a condition. Not one of the four names a human being outright — and that is the ordinary state of affairs in every language, once you start pulling the words open.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{la enfermera}, then \emph{el enfermero}
  \item \emph{enfermo} and \emph{enfermera}, and hear the patient inside the nurse
  \item \emph{la enfermera} and \emph{el maestro}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What are the pieces of \emph{infirmus}? (\emph{In-}, not, and \emph{firmus}, firm.) Who is the nurse named after? (The patient.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[el cocinero]{el cocinero — the root that got everywhere}

\label{lesson:ES-C285-cocinero}



\begin{quote}
Before the last of the five: who is the nurse named after? (The patient.) And what is \emph{magis}? (More.)
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item la comida — what this person makes.
  \item la enfermera — the person before this one.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{co-ci-NE-ro}, stress on the \emph{ne}. The first \emph{c} is a hard \emph{k} and the second, before \emph{i}, is soft. $\to$ reference
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{el cocinero} — \textquotedblleft{}the cook.\textquotedblright{}

From \textbf{la cocina}, the kitchen — Latin \textbf{coquina} — and under that \textbf{coquere}, to cook.

This root travelled further than any other in the run. English \textbf{kitchen} is \emph{coquina}, borrowed into Germanic early and worn right down. A \textbf{biscuit} is \emph{bis-coctus}, twice-cooked. To \textbf{concoct} is to cook things together. And a \textbf{precocious} child is \emph{prae-coquus}, cooked early — a word used first of fruit that ripened before its season, and moved onto children only much later.

So the same Latin root gave English a room, a snack, a metaphor for scheming and a word for a clever eight-year-old, and gave Spanish the person who does the cooking.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
Five people: \emph{el vecino}, \emph{la amiga}, \emph{el maestro}, \emph{la enfermera}, \emph{el cocinero}.

Set the five descriptions side by side. \emph{Vecino} is a place. \emph{Amiga} is a feeling. \emph{Maestro} is a comparison. \emph{Enfermera} is a condition. \emph{Cocinero} is an action. Five ways of pointing at a person without ever saying what a person is.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{el cocinero}, then \emph{la cocinera}
  \item \emph{la cocina} and \emph{el cocinero}, the room and the person
  \item all five in order — \emph{el vecino}, \emph{la amiga}, \emph{el maestro}, \emph{la enfermera}, \emph{el cocinero}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is a \emph{biscuit}, taken apart? (Twice-cooked.) What does \emph{precocious} literally mean? (Cooked early.) And who is the \emph{enfermera} named after? (The patient.)
\end{tcolorbox}
